literal: The wrath sing, goddess, of Peleus's-son Achilles, ruinous, which countless upon-the-Achaeans woes placed, and many mighty souls to-Hades sent-forth of-heroes, and-them-themselves made prey for-dogs and-for-birds all, and-of-Zeus was-being-fulfilled the plan, from which indeed first stood-apart-both having-striven-both Atreus's-son and lord of-men and godlike Achilles. Who, then, of the gods brought the two of them together in strife to fight? of-Leto and of-Zeus [the] son; For he, having become angry at the king, raised up an evil plague throughout the army, and the people were perishing, because the-son-of-Atreus dishonored Chryses the priest. For he came to the swift ships of-the-Achaeans, about-to-ransom his-daughter and bringing boundless ransoms, holding fillets in his-hands of far-shooting Apollo upon a golden staff, and he-was-beseeching all the-Achaeans, but the-two-sons-of-Atreus especially, the-two marshals of-the-peoples. Sons-of-Atreus and other well-greaved Achaeans, to you may the gods who hold Olympian homes grant to sack the city of Priam, and well homeward to arrive; My dear daughter release to me, and the ransom accept, revering Zeus's son, far-shooting Apollo. Then all the other Achaeans shouted assent, both to respect the priest and to accept the splendid ransom; but [it] was not pleasing to Atreus's-son Agamemnon in [his] heart, but he was sending [him] away badly, and moreover he was enjoining [his] stern word upon [him]: Not you, old man, by the hollow ships may I find, either now lingering or later again coming, lest now for you not it may avail—the staff and the wreath of the god; Her but I not will-release; Before, even old age will come upon her in our house, in Argos, far from [her] fatherland, plying the loom and meeting my bed; But go, do not provoke me, safer, so that you may return.
prose: Sing, goddess, of the ruinous wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus, which brought countless sorrows upon the Achaeans, and sent many valiant souls of heroes down to Hades, and made the men themselves prey for dogs and all birds, while the plan of Zeus was being fulfilled — from the time when first Atreus' son, lord of men, and godlike Achilles parted in strife. Which of the gods, then, brought the two of them together to fight in strife? The son of Leto and Zeus. For he, angered at the king, raised an evil plague throughout the army, and the people were dying, because the son of Atreus had dishonored the priest Chryses. For he had come to the swift ships of the Achaeans to ransom his daughter, bringing countless ransoms, holding in his hands the fillets of far-shooting Apollo upon a golden staff, and he beseeched all the Achaeans, but especially the two sons of Atreus, marshals of the people. Sons of Atreus and you other well-greaved Achaeans, may the gods who hold Olympian homes grant you to sack Priam's city and return home safely. Release my dear daughter to me, and accept the ransom, out of reverence for Zeus's son, far-shooting Apollo. Then all the other Achaeans shouted assent, bidding him respect the priest and accept the splendid ransom; but it did not please the heart of Agamemnon, son of Atreus; instead, he dismissed him harshly and laid upon him a stern command. Old man, do not let me find you by the hollow ships, either lingering now or coming back again later, lest your staff and the god's wreath fail to protect you. But her I will not release. Before that, old age will come upon her in our house, far from her homeland in Argos, as she tends the loom and shares my bed. But go, do not provoke me, so that you may return the safer.

literal: So he spoke, and the old man was afraid and obeyed [his] word. He went, [and] silent, along [the] shore of-the-loud-roaring sea. And then, going apart, [he] prayed many [things] to lord Apollo, the old man, whom fair-haired Leto bore: Hear me, silver-bowed one, who Chrysa have-stood-around, and Cilla the holy, and of-Tenedos with-might you-rule, Smintheus, if ever for-you a pleasing temple I-roofed, or if indeed ever for-you down the fat thigh-pieces I-burned of-bulls and of-goats, this for-me fulfill, [my] wish: may the Danaans pay-for my tears with your arrows. Thus he spoke praying, and him Phoebus Apollo heard, and he went down from [the] peaks of Olympus, raging at heart, [his] bow on [his] shoulders having, and [his] covered quiver. And then the arrows rattled upon the shoulders of [him] raging, of him himself having been moved. He [went] on his way, being like to night. He sat down then apart from-the ships, and he let-go an arrow. Terrible [was] the twang became of the silver bow. The mules indeed first he went upon, and the swift dogs, but then, sending upon them [his] sharp-piercing arrow, he kept striking. Always and pyres of-corpses were-being-burned frequent. For-nine-days indeed throughout the army went the shafts of-the-god, on-the tenth [day] and called [to] assembly the people Achilles. For in [his] mind [the] white-armed goddess Hera placed-it [i.e. that word/intent]. For he cared for [the] Danaans, because indeed he saw [them] dying. And they, when then they had been gathered and became assembled together, then among them rising up swift of feet Achilles spoke: Son of Atreus, now us, having been driven back again, I think [us] back will return home, if indeed death we might escape, if indeed together war and plague overpower the Achaeans. But come now, let us ask some seer or priest or even a dream-interpreter—for a dream too is from Zeus—who might say why so greatly Phoebus Apollo has grown angry, whether, then, he blames [us] for a vow and a hecatomb, if somehow, having met with the savor of lambs and unblemished goats, he wishes to ward off ruin from us.
prose: So he spoke, and the old man was afraid and obeyed his word. He went in silence along the shore of the loud-roaring sea. Then, going apart, the old man prayed earnestly to lord Apollo, whom fair-haired Leto bore: "Hear me, god of the silver bow, you who guard Chrysa and holy Cilla and rule Tenedos with might, Smintheus! If ever I roofed a pleasing temple for you, or if ever I burned the fat thigh-bones of bulls and goats for you, grant me this wish: may the Danaans pay for my tears with your arrows." So he spoke in prayer, and Phoebus Apollo heard him, and came down from the peaks of Olympus, enraged at heart, with his bow upon his shoulders and his covered quiver. The arrows rattled on the shoulders of the angry god as he moved, and he went like night. Then he sat down apart from the ships and let fly an arrow, and terrible was the twang of the silver bow. First he went after the mules and swift dogs, but then, aiming his sharp arrow at the men themselves, he struck them, and continually the frequent pyres of the dead burned. For nine days the god's shafts ranged through the army, and on the tenth day Achilles called the people to assembly—for the white-armed goddess Hera had put that thought in his mind, since she cared for the Danaans, because she saw them dying. And when they had gathered and were assembled, swift-footed Achilles rose among them and spoke: "Son of Atreus, now I think that we, driven back again, will return home, if indeed we should escape death, that is, if war and plague together are to overpower the Achaeans. But come, let us ask some seer or priest, or even an interpreter of dreams—for a dream too comes from Zeus—who might tell us why Phoebus Apollo is so greatly angered, whether he blames us for a vow or a hecatomb left unpaid, and whether, if he somehow accepts the savor of lambs and unblemished goats, he may be willing to ward off this plague from us."

literal: Verily he, having spoken thus, sat down then; among them rose Calchas Thestorides, of bird-diviners far the best, who knew the things being and the things about-to-be and the things being before, and [who] led the ships of-the-Achaeans into Ilium by his prophetic-art, which to-him gave Phoebus Apollo; he, well disposed toward them, spoke-in-assembly and addressed-[them] [among them]: O Achilles, you bid me, [you] dear to Zeus, declare the wrath of Apollo the far-shooting lord; for I will tell them, I; but you agree and swear to me, truly indeed that you, to me, [being] well-disposed, with words and with hands, will help; yes, for I think [that] I will anger the man, who mightily over all the Argives holds power, and him the Achaeans obey; for stronger [is] a king, when he grows angry with a lesser man; for even if indeed he digests his wrath on the very day, yet still even afterward he holds anger, until he accomplishes [it], in his own breast; but you, declare whether you will save me. Him answering swift-footed Achilles addressed: Having taken courage, speak out fully the prophecy, whatever you know; no, for by Apollo dear to Zeus, to whom you, Calchas, praying, reveal prophecies to the Danaans, no one of all the Danaans together, while I am living and looking upon the earth, will bring heavy hands upon you beside the hollow ships, not even if you should name Agamemnon, who now claims to be by far best of the Achaeans.
prose: So when he had spoken thus, he sat down; and among them rose Calchas son of Thestor, far the best of bird-diviners, who knew the things that are, the things to come, and the things that had been before, and who had guided the ships of the Achaeans to Ilium by the gift of prophecy that Phoebus Apollo had given him. He, with good will toward them, spoke among them and addressed them: "Achilles, dear to Zeus, you bid me declare the wrath of lord Apollo, the far-shooter. For I will tell you these things. But do you agree and swear to me that you will indeed readily help me with words and with hands. Yes, for I think I will anger the man who rules mightily over all the Argives, and whom the Achaeans obey. For a king is stronger when he is angry with a lesser man. For even if he digests his wrath for that day, yet he still keeps his anger thereafter, until he fulfills it, in his own breast. But tell me whether you will save me." Swift-footed Achilles answered him and said: "Take courage and tell me whatever prophecy you know. No, by Apollo dear to Zeus, to whom you, Calchas, pray and reveal prophecies to the Danaans, no one of all the Danaans, while I live and look upon the earth, will lay heavy hands on you beside the hollow ships, not even if you name Agamemnon, who now claims to be by far the best of the Achaeans.

literal: And then indeed he-took-courage and was-speaking, [the] blameless seer: not, then, [is] he at all aggrieved on account of a vow nor of a hecatomb, but on account of the priest whom Agamemnon dishonored, and did not release [his] daughter and did not accept ransoms, for that reason indeed the Far-shooter gave griefs and still will give [them].
prose: And then indeed the blameless seer took courage and spoke: "It is not, then, over a vow or a hecatomb that he is aggrieved, but because of the priest whom Agamemnon dishonored, and did not release his daughter nor accept the ransom—therefore the Far-shooter gave us griefs, and will yet give more."

literal: Him then, answering, addressed mighty Agamemnon: "Not thus, good though being, godlike Achilles, be-deceiving in mind, since not you-will-get-past nor me will-you-persuade. Truly do you wish that you yourself may have [your] prize, but that I sit thus idly, being deprived, and do you bid me give back this [girl]? But if indeed the great-hearted Achaeans will give [me] a prize, having fitted [it] according to [their] heart, so that it will be a fitting-in-return [one]; but if they should not give [it], I myself will take [it], going, either yours or Ajax's prize, or Odysseus's I will lead away, having taken [it]. He will-be-angry, whomever I-may-come-to. But indeed these things we will discuss again again; but now come, the black ship let us drag into the sacred sea, and in it let us gather rowers for the purpose, and into it let us place a hecatomb, and up into it let us bring fair-cheeked Chryseis herself. But let some one man be leader, a counsel-bearing man, either Ajax or Idomeneus or godlike Odysseus or you, son of Peleus, most formidable of all men, so that for us you may propitiate the one who works from afar, having performed sacred rites." Him then [him] looking askance [at], addressed [him] swift of feet Achilles: "Woe to me, [you who are] clad in shamelessness, scheming-minded one, how might any of the Achaeans, willing, obey [you] with [your] words, either to go on a journey or to fight men by might? Not for I I-for-the-sake-of-Trojans spearmen came hither about-to-fight, since not at-all to-me blameworthy they-are; for not ever yet did they drive off my cattle, nor indeed my horses, nor ever in Phthia of the rich soil, nurse of men, did they damage the harvest, since truly very many [things lie] between—both shadowy mountains and the resounding sea. But for-you, O greatly-shameless-one, together we-followed, in-order-that you might-rejoice, honor winning for-Menelaus and for-you, dog-face, against [the] Trojans. Of these [things] not at all do you turn yourself about, nor do you take heed. And indeed you yourself threaten to take away from me [my] prize, for which I toiled much, and the sons of the Achaeans gave [it] to me. Not indeed to-you ever equal I-have a-prize, whenever the-Achaeans of-the-Trojans sack a-well-inhabited citadel. But the greater [part] of much-rushing war my hands manage—but if ever a distribution/division comes, to you the prize [is] much greater, I but a small and dear [one] having go to the ships, when I grow weary making war. But now I will go to Phthia, since truly [it is] far better to go home with curved ships, nor do I think, [being] dishonored here, that I will draw off wealth and riches for you."
prose: Answering him, powerful Agamemnon said: "Do not try to deceive me with your mind this way, godlike Achilles, good though you are, since you will not get past me or persuade me. Do you really wish to keep your own prize while I sit idly by, deprived of mine, and you bid me give this one back? But if the great-hearted Achaeans will give me a prize, fitting it to my heart's content so that it will be a fair match—but if they do not give it, then I myself will go and take a prize, either yours or Ajax's, or I will seize and carry off Odysseus's. Whoever he be to whom I come will be angry. Well, we will discuss these matters again later; but now come, let us drag the black ship down into the sacred sea, gather rowers for it on purpose, put aboard a hecatomb, and bring fair-cheeked Chryseis herself aboard. Let some one man be our leader and counselor—either Ajax, or Idomeneus, or godlike Odysseus, or you, son of Peleus, most formidable of all men—so that you may appease the god who strikes from afar by performing sacred rites." Looking at him darkly, swift-footed Achilles said to him: "Shame on you, clothed in shamelessness, you schemer—how can any of the Achaeans willingly obey your words, whether to go on a journey or to fight men with strength? For I did not come here to fight for the sake of the Trojan spearmen, since they are not at all to blame for me; for they never once drove off my cattle or my horses, nor ever in deep-soiled, man-nourishing Phthia did they ravage the harvest, since truly there lies between us much—shadowy mountains and the resounding sea. But it was for you, oh shameless one, that we followed, so that you might rejoice, winning honor for Menelaus and for you, dog-face, against the Trojans. You care nothing at all for these, nor do you give them a thought. And now you threaten to take away my prize yourself, the very one for which I toiled hard—the sons of the Achaeans gave it to me. I never have a prize equal to yours, whenever the Achaeans sack some well-inhabited Trojan citadel. But the greater part of the tumultuous war my hands manage—but if ever a distribution of spoils comes, your prize is much greater, while I go off to the ships with a small and dear one, whenever I grow weary of fighting. But now I will go to Phthia, since it is far better to go home with my curved ships, and I do not think that, dishonored as I am here, I will draw off wealth and riches for you."

literal: Him then answered [the] lord of men Agamemnon: Flee very much, if to-you heart is-set-in-motion, nor do I at-least beseech [you], for-the-sake-of me, to-remain. Beside me [there-are] also others who will-honor me, and most-of-all Zeus the-counselor. Most-hateful indeed to-me you-are of Zeus-nurtured kings; for always to-you strife [is] dear, and wars and battles. If very strong you-are, a-god, I-suppose, gave that to-you. Homeward going, with ships both yours and your comrades the-Myrmidons, be-lord; but of-you I take no account, nor do I care for [you] being-angry. And I-will-threaten, to-you, thus: as from-me takes-away Chryseis Phoebus Apollo, her indeed I will-send with my ship and with my companions, but I, I will-lead Briseis beautiful-cheeked, going myself to [your] hut, your prize, so-that you-may-know well how-much mightier I-am than-you, and [so-that] another also may-dread [himself] equal to-me to-say and to-be-made-like [to-me] face-to-face. Thus he-spoke. To-the-son-of-Peleus grief came, and in [to] him [his] heart in [his] shaggy breast in-two-ways pondered, whether he, the sharp sword having-drawn from beside [his] thigh, should-make the-others rise-up, and he the-son-of-Atreus should-slay, or should-stop [his] wrath and should-restrain [his] spirit. While he these-things was-pondering in [his] mind and in [his] heart, he-was-drawing from [its] sheath [his] great sword, and came Athena from-heaven; for forth [her] sent the-goddess white-armed Hera, both alike in-heart loving [them] and caring [for-them]. She-stood behind [him], and by [his] golden hair she-seized the-son-of-Peleus, appearing to [him] alone. Of-the others, no-one was-seen. He-was-astonished—Achilles—and he-turned-around after[ward], and at-once he-recognized Pallas Athena; terrible [dual] his [dative] two-eyes appeared. And him, having-spoken, [with] winged words he-addressed: Why again, of aegis-bearing Zeus [you] child, have-you-come? Truly, [is-it] in-order-that he-might-see the-insolence of-Agamemnon, son-of-Atreus? But out to-you I-will-speak, and-this I-think also to-be-being-fulfilled: by [his] own acts-of-arrogance, perhaps he might some-day lose [his] life.
prose: Then lord of men Agamemnon answered him: "Flee, by all means, if your heart drives you to it; I for my part do not beg you to stay for my sake. Others are at my side who will honor me, above all Zeus the counselor. You are the most hateful to me of kings cherished by Zeus, for strife and wars and battles are ever dear to you. If you are very strong, some god, I suppose, gave you that. Go home with your own ships and your own comrades, and be lord over the Myrmidons; I care nothing for you, nor do I regard your anger. And I will threaten you thus: since Phoebus Apollo is taking Chryseis from me, her I will send away with my ship and my companions, but I myself will go to your hut and take fair-cheeked Briseis, your prize, so that you may know well how much mightier I am than you, and that another too may dread to claim equality with me and to compare himself to me face to face." So he spoke, and grief came upon the son of Peleus, and within his shaggy breast his heart pondered two ways: whether, drawing the sharp sword from beside his thigh, he should make the others rise and slay the son of Atreus, or should check his wrath and restrain his spirit. While he pondered these things in mind and heart, and was drawing his great sword from its sheath, Athena came down from heaven, for the white-armed goddess Hera had sent her forth, loving and caring for both men alike in her heart. She stood behind him and, appearing to him alone, caught the son of Peleus by his golden hair. None of the others saw her. Achilles was astonished, and turned around, and at once recognized Pallas Athena; terribly her eyes blazed. And speaking to her he said: "Why have you come again, child of aegis-bearing Zeus? Is it to see the insolence of Agamemnon, son of Atreus? But I will tell you plainly, and I think this too will come to pass: through his own acts of arrogance he may perhaps one day lose his life."
